title: I let AI become my interior designer. Here’s what happened
source_used: London Evening Standard (pre-fetched full text; first-person feature)
key_facts: A London Evening Standard writer (not named in the text) used AI chatbots and visualisation apps while renovating a new house in east London and choosing a new colour for its 'funny blue' exterior.

The writer found chatbots gave no real help with furnishings and colours, repeating 'Scandi cool' and 'mid-century chic' and producing endless lists; apps such as IdealHouse and Homevisualizer AI did somewhat better, though few worked.

ChatGPT (which rarely managed to render an image) and Google Gemini were used to picture the house in Farrow & Ball greens; asking again for the same shade gave a completely different image each time.
Paint testers bought at B&Q looked nothing like the AI images; the family picked a green far bolder than first imagined and is reasonably happy, though it looks nothing like the renders.

Catherine Seagrave, design director and co-founder of the online interiors agency the Living House, says AI is brilliant at giving 20 ideas but less good at knowing which is right, and advises checking measurements, ordering samples and not letting it make expensive or permanent decisions.
The article cites research by furniture retailer Barker and Stonehouse that 61 per cent of UK adults have used AI for interior design inspiration, 88 per cent among 25- to 34-year-olds.
KDS Interiors is quoted as saying interior designers can cost as much as £450 an hour.
quote_evidence: AI is brilliant at giving you 20 different ideas. It is less good at knowing which idea is the right one,

Research published last month by furniture retailers Barker and Stonehouse found that some 61 per cent of UK adults have used AI for interior design inspiration, rising to 88 per cent among 25- to 34-year-olds.
We are reasonably happy with the end result, although it certainly looks nothing like any of the renders.
why_it_matters_hint: Many people now use AI for home decisions, but this account shows it can be unreliable on colour and fit, so a designer's judgement still matters.
